11674-the-torrent-entre-naranjos:
Vicente Blasco Ibáñez's The Torrent, translated by Isaac Goldberg and Arthur Livingston in 1921, opens with Rafael, a young deputy back from Madrid, greeted at the club and at home. His mother Doña Bernarda watches him with deep, severe, maternal eyes.

Rafael strides from a dining room where coffee is still being sipped, down a broad red marble stair, into the silence of an ancient mansion. Later scenes bring a blonde beauty with large green eyes, her bearded father, and a city cold and bustling against warm orchards. The novel is a Spanish story of politics, family, and return.
13672-the-unknown-eros:
Coventry Patmore's poetry collection, gathered in a third edition that adds his other poems in what he calls catalectic verse, where pauses do much of the work of metre. The poems are religious and personal, turning on love, marriage, faith, and the soul, written in a high, musical style that leans on rhyme and rhythm.

Later sections move between satire and devotion, mocking public figures and praising married love as a path to the divine. Patmore's language is ornate and sometimes obscure, but the feeling is direct: earthly love, rightly kept, mirrors heavenly love. The book stands as a late Victorian statement of Catholic faith expressed through domestic feeling.
14391-the-cattle-raid-of-cualnge-tain-bo:
L. Winifred Faraday translated this old Irish prose epic, the Cattle Raid of Cualnge, in 1904. She worked from the Book of the Dun Cow and the Yellow Book of Lecan, two old manuscripts. None of the three copies, she notes, descends straight from another. The Leinster scribe aimed to be clear, while the other scribes aimed to be exact. The epic tells of Queen Medb's raid for the Brown Bull of Cualnge.

Medb's host ravages Cualnge and seeks the Bull in the places of Sliab Culind. The river Cronn rises to the tree tops against them, and they spend a night by its banks. A warrior named Ualu tries to cross with a stone on his back, but the stream drives him back, and his grave stands by the road. Cuchulainn piles fences of corpses round the host, three deep, in a slaughter the epic counts among its wonders.
14660-mabini-s-decalogue-for-filipinos:
Mabini's Decalogue for Filipinos, issued by the Philippine Press Bureau in Washington in 1922, prints Apolinario Mabini's ten precepts for his people beside a short life of the man. Mabini is called the most profound thinker the Filipino race ever produced.

The first precept bids Filipinos love their country after God and their honor, and more than themselves. She is their only paradise in this life, their ancestors' inheritance, and their posterity's hope. Born at Tanauan, Batangas, in 1864, Mabini was imprisoned from September 1899 to September 1900 and kept writing through paralysis and poverty. The pamphlet is a compact patriotic classic.
14968-the-standard-operas-their-plots-th:
George P. Upton's handbook, in a twelfth edition from McClurg in 1897, sketches standard operas likely to be given in regular seasons, with plots, music and composers. Its preface explains that Upton consulted the best authorities, added his own observations, and gave a brief sketch of each composer.

For each opera he tells the story, describes the general character of the music and notes famous numbers, so a listener can follow a performance without a full score. The handbook suits opera goers, students and programme writers. Upton's choices shaped what American audiences counted as standard repertory in the late nineteenth century.
17349-frank-among-the-rancheros:
Harry Castlemon, author of the Gun-Boat and Go-Ahead series, wrote this Rocky Mountain tale for young readers, published by the John C. Winston Company. Frank, the hero of earlier Castlemon books, finds a new home among rancheros. The chapters promise a novel battle, twelve thousand dollars, a fight in court, and proof that Frank is a hero. A highwayman, Colonel Arthur Vane, and Pierre and his band soon complicate matters.

The story runs on through treachery, an escape, and a struggle on a cliff, in Castlemon's brisk boys' adventure style. Readers get a western tale of ranch life, danger, and pluck, written for the young audience that followed Frank from book to book. It stands as a sturdy example of nineteenth-century adventure fiction for boys.
18352-captured-by-the-navajos:
Captain Charles A. Curtis of the United States Army wrote this boys' adventure, published by Harper and Brothers in New York and London in 1904, with illustrations. A frontispiece shows every man holding his rifle ready to shoot escaping Apaches. Curtis, a soldier writing for boys, sets his tale among army posts, Navajo country, and Apache trails in the Southwest.

Chapters introduce the boys, then attack by Navajos, warlike Pueblos, a Navajo trap, a siege and ambuscade, and crossing a river. A swollen stream, a stolen pony, a missing corporal, and a rescuing party follow, with both ponies stolen and Indians on the war path. Later chapters cross a desert without water and pursue Apaches into Skull Valley. Readers get a frontier army story: boys learning soldiering, scouting, and courage on the trail.
25294-chats-on-household-curios:
Fred W. Burgess's Chats on Household Curios, published by T. Fisher Unwin, is a collector's guide with 94 illustrations. It belongs to a popular series that chatted about china, furniture, prints, lace, pewter, stamps, and coins for readers of moderate means.

Burgess shows old fireplaces with Sussex backs, andirons, and trivets, then turns to ivories from Africa, India, China, and Japan, carved and inlaid into furniture and ornaments. Miniature kettles and gilt jewels illustrate the range of household curios. The book helps beginners tell genuine old pieces from later copies. Burgess writes for collectors who hunt old shops and auctions on modest budgets.
25512-the-fables-of-ph-drus-literally-tr:
Henry Thomas Riley renders the fables of Phaedrus into plain English prose, with notes drawn from the little known about the Roman author's life and times. Familiar tales appear in order, including the Wolf and the Lamb, the Frogs Asking for a King, the Fox and the Tragic Mask, and the Wolf and the Crane.

Christopher Smart's metrical version stands beside Riley's prose, so readers can compare a close rendering with a verse retelling of the same fables. Footnotes grouped after each book explain names, customs, and points of Latin usage for readers without Latin.
27013-hellhounds-of-the-cosmos:
Clifford D. Simak's Hellhounds of the Cosmos throws Earth into an interdimensional struggle, faced by Dr. White and his ninety-nine men. The Black Horror has already wiped out Six Corners, a hamlet in Pennsylvania, and sent natives fleeing down the Amazon in babbling fear.

When London reports thousands of the creatures surrounding the city and martial rule declared, a newspaper editor stops the presses for a new front page. Simak's pulp nightmare moves from newsroom panic to strange science, as humanity learns what kind of enemy has slipped between worlds.
30457-through-russian-snows-a-story-of-n:
G. A. Henty writes Through Russian Snows, a story of Napoleon's retreat from Moscow, copyrighted in 1895 and published in New York in 1902 with eight illustrations and three maps. Contents open with two brothers, a hearing before justices, a fresh scrape, and a smuggler's cave.

Later chapters follow a trail, a commission, a French prison, and pistol scenes, as a boy hero moves through war and capture. An illustration shows Sergeant Julian Wyatt receiving the Cross of the Legion of Honour. Henty pairs adventure with history, teaching young readers about the Russian winter, French armies, and courage under hardship.
31423-in-door-gardening-for-every-week-i:
William Keane's In-Door Gardening for Every Week in the Year appeared in a third edition published in London in 1865. It shows the most successful treatment for all plants cultivated in the greenhouse, conservatory, stove, pit, orchid, and forcing-house. The book is organized week by week through the year, beginning with January's first week. Its greenhouse and conservatory advice covers cinerarias, which need a final shift and room to expand, and epacrises preparing to burst into flower.

Keane writes for gardeners who kept tender plants indoors through English winters. Each week's entry tells the reader what to shift, tie, water, and watch. The book is a practical Victorian manual, still useful as a record of greenhouse practice. Readers with a conservatory, or an interest in one, will find its weekly rhythm both charming and instructive.
32017-company-k-twentieth-regiment-illin:
Andrew Brown's roster and record of Company K, Twentieth Regiment, Illinois Volunteer Infantry, was printed at Yorkville, Illinois, in 1894. Its title page spans April 24, 1861, to July 16, 1865. Brown took on the work at the survivors' reunion in Chicago on September 8, 1893, when the regimental association asked him to prepare the company's roster. He wrote it for surviving members, their descendants, and relatives of men who had died.

The book is a reference work, not a campaign narrative. Its entries follow individual soldiers, giving birthplace, enlistment place and date, rank, and service notes. The opening entry, Captain Reuben F. Dyer of Ottawa, shows the pattern: he volunteered at Newark in April 1861, commanded at Fort Henry and Fort Donelson and at Fredericktown, and resigned his captaincy in March 1862. Genealogists and Civil War researchers will find it most useful as a company roll.
33729-the-lost-temples-of-xantoos: Howell Calhoun's sonnet The Lost Temples of Xantoos, published in Weird Tales in October 1936, pictures ruined Martian temples in fourteen lines. Undying night, pearl-adorned colonnades, and glowing crimson guardians tower over huge ruins on a shore once washed by Xantoos' rolling seas. Nothing remains on that barren core of Mars but palatial memories. Altars, magnificent black gods, sapphire torches, sacred flowers, jeweled gates, and a lurid shadow complete the vision.
34683-intra-muros:
Rebecca Ruter Springer wrote Intra Muros, published at Elgin, Illinois, in 1898 by the David Cook Publishing Company. Her preface insists the pages hold no fancy sketch written to pass an idle hour. They are the true, though greatly condensed, record of an experience during days when her life hung in the balance between time and eternity, with the scales dipping decidedly toward eternity. She doubts she can paint the scenes for others as they appeared to her.

Springer describes a vision of heaven seen during a grave illness: its streets, music, and meetings with the dead. The book, known as Within the Gates in later printings, comforted generations of readers.
34732-max-carrados:
Ernest Bramah published this set of detective stories with Methuen in London in 1914. Its hero, Max Carrados, is a blind amateur detective, and the eight tales in the contents list send him after coins, signals, and cottage tragedies.

The first case opens in a coin shop, where an inquiry agent named Carlyle shows the dealer Baxter a Sicilian tetradrachm of Dionysius. The coin is said to have fetched two hundred and fifty pounds at a famous sale. Later cases turn on a knight's cross signal problem, the clever Mrs. Straithwaite, an actor's last exploit, and a game played in the dark. Bramah lets Carrados work by ear, touch, and sharp reasoning, which sets him apart from the keen eyed sleuths of his day.
35433-observations-on-mount-vesuvius-mou:
Sir William Hamilton sent these letters on volcanos to the Royal Society while he served as British envoy at Naples. A new edition, with fresh notes by Hamilton, came out in London in 1774. Hamilton watched Vesuvius from his arrival in Naples in late 1764. A great eruption soon gave him much to report.

Letter by letter, he tells what he saw with his own eyes. Smoke thickened before bad weather, and deep blasts could be heard in the city. He climbed the cone, noted lava, ash, and the changing crater. Etna and other volcanos enter for comparison. Hamilton leaves deep causes to men of science, but his plain eyewitness record became a base text for the study of volcanos.
39428-a-hymn-on-the-life-virtues-and-mir:
A Hymn on the Life, Virtues, and Miracles of Saint Patrick was composed by his disciple Saint Fiech, bishop of Sletty. The print gives the Irish original on one page with an English version of the whole facing it. A Latin version, from Colgan collection of the patron saint lives, stands at the foot of each page.

The editor says the work prints not only to clear up the apostle history but also to please lovers of Irish letters. It is a specimen of the language spoken in Ireland about twelve hundred years before. In the English version, the plain sense and the turns of the words and phrases are kept where the editor and his Gaelic Society helpers could fully grasp them. Short notes clear the text. Church and language fans get a three tongue hymn.
39435-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Part of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica stands here, the slice of the alphabet that runs from Helmont onward. Fine print and dense columns mark the great 1911 reference work.

The opening pages carry the editors' own list of small print fixes. They correct the articles on Hemimorphite, a zinc ore found in limestone beds. The Hemp article gains a fixed line on the drug as an intoxicant. Henley's Views and Reviews is called a mosaic of scraps in its own patched quote. Henry the Eighth, the Herbarium, and Hercules all earn small repairs. Later pages hold the full articles themselves. Readers get the famed reference set in its own careful voice.
39910-omphalos:
Philip Henry Gosse wrote this book, printed in London in 1857. Its full title calls it an attempt to untie the knot of the science of the earth. It holds fifty-six cuts on wood. A line from Aristotle in Greek stands on the title page, on growth through the navel. The first pages tell a tale from the author's youth. He was a clerk in Newfoundland some five and twenty years past, when a brig of his firm was wrecked.

The tale turns on a point of the craft of the sea. The master of the brig had fixed his place by the sun the day before, north of a cape. Fog came on, and he sailed by the compass in trust of that fix. At night the ship struck the cliffs far to the south of where he thought he was.
40188-love-in-the-suds-a-town-eclogue-be:
Love in the Suds is a town eclogue, the lamentation of Roscius for the loss of his Nyky. It is printed with a letter from William Kenrick to the actor David Garrick. This third edition was printed at London in 1772. Kenrick begins with a Latin shrug: written with his god angry with him.

The author of the eclogue, Kenrick writes, asked help to introduce it to the world. Kenrick then learned, with indignation, that Garrick had used his influence over the press to keep it from being advertised. How is Garrick concerned in this lamentation, he demands. Does Garrick think no man is entitled to the name of Roscius but himself? The verse satire and its truculent preface belong to the pamphlet wars of the Georgian stage.
40575-the-great-commission-miscellaneous:
The Great Commission is the fourth volume of the miscellaneous writings of Mackintosh. Loizeaux Brothers published the collection in New York. Its first article asks a plain question: what is conversion? The writer studies the first chapter of First Thessalonians for an answer. That chapter gives a picture of genuine conversion, he holds. He proposes to study the picture in company with the reader. The answer should be distinct and clear, he promises.

He insists on the universal necessity of divine conversion. Let a man be Jew or Greek, Protestant or Roman Catholic, he writes. Whatever his nationality or creed, he must be converted. Else he is on the broad road to an everlasting hell. No one is born a Christian in the true sense, he argues. The volume gathers evangelical teaching papers in Mackintosh's manner.
41156-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
The Encyclopaedia Britannica, eleventh edition, here a part volume running in its article sequence from Japan toward Jeveros, holds the long article Japan and the entries that follow it. A transcriber note lists corrections made to the Japan article. Korean history names twenty five raids made by the Japanese against Silla in the first five centuries of the Christian era, the article notes. None can be identified with Jingo alleged expedition, it holds.

Where agents of central power found themselves impotent, petty chieftains of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries could accomplish nothing, the article argues. The survivors of a later war fled to Osaka, where Hideyori sheltered behind ramparts held by eighty thousand men. History, geography, arts, and modern growth fill the Japan article at length. Reference readers get the great nineteen eleven Britannica on Japan in full.
42250-dave-dawson-with-the-commandos:
Dave Dawson with the Commandos, by Bowen, appeared in 1942, in the middle of the Second World War, as one of a long series of boys' aviation novels. Dave Dawson and his friend Freddy Farmer are both young fliers. They finish an enormous meal as the story opens. Strange orders soon send them eastward to England and into danger.

The chapters promise night attacks, a dead man's wings, invisible death, and a vulture's nest, as the two heroes join commando style operations against the Nazis. Bowen wrote the Dawson books at speed for young readers eager for war news in story form, and this entry delivers the series' usual mix of flying, secret missions, and nerve.
42522-extracts-from-the-diary-and-corres:
Extracts from the Diary and Correspondence of Amos Lawrence presents the private papers of a famed Boston merchant. His son, William R Lawrence, a physician, edited the book. Gould and Lincoln published it in Boston in 1856, a few years after the elder Lawrence's death. The editor inscribed it to his uncle, the merchant's only surviving brother.

Among the papers lay copies of many letters Lawrence wrote to his children. He had kept them so his counsel might guide their children after him. The family first printed one hundred copies for private use. The son then prepared this fuller selection from the letters and a daily diary. Lawrence was known for vast gifts to colleges and charities. The book shows the faith and discipline behind the fortune.
4309-demos:
George Gissing set this novel first at Stanbury Hill, above a green valley near the Severn untouched by mine, factory, and furnace. At its foot lies Wanley, a village of stone houses with mullioned windows, gables, and old chimneys. The oldest building there anchors a story of old England meeting new industry.

Demos, the people as a political force, enters through an heir, a fortune, and the clash of classes that follows. Gissing follows workers, owners, and idealists as money changes hands and hopes. An editor's note warns that two chapters share the number twenty-six, an error found in other print copies as well.
43159-two-studios:
Frances Peard's Two Studios was published by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, in an edition dated 1887. Peard opens with a hunt for art's hiding-places in London. Off a broad, sordid thoroughfare, a rusty entrance leads to a long court with twelve old pollarded trees in leaf.

That court is the threshold of another world: hard work and heart-burning, but also the joy of beauty and the push to create. On one side stand the painters with their colours and draperies; on the other, cold marble and the workmen who carry out a master's thought. Charles Everitt, a painter five years settled there, calls it the most delightful spot in the world.
48366-chats-on-military-curios:
Stanley C Johnson wrote Chats on Military Curios, with eighty pictures, issued at New York by Frederick A Stokes Company as part of a Books for Collectors set. A bronze medallion of the Duke of Wellington forms the front print. Front pages list mate volumes on china, furniture, prints, costume, lace, and coins.

Johnson held degrees in arts and science and a post in a learned society. The Chats series aimed to teach collectors how to know and value old goods. Military curios in this volume span arms, medals, dress, and relics of war. Plain talk, not deep study, is the mode of the series. Readers get hints on what to seek, what to shun, and how prices are set. The book is given in brief as To G M J on its dedication page.
49631-cosmos:
Cosmos, by Ernest McGaffey, is a long poem on life, faith, and man. The Philosopher Press of Wausau, Wisconsin, issued it with rights in 1903. A dedication to Carter Harrison of Chicago fronts the verse in full. Part one asks who has solved the riddle of life or death.

Creed after creed is piled like Etna on Vesuvius, then cast aside. Priest made doctrine reads grotesque to the poet, east or west alike. Man did not descend from the ape, the poem insists in plain terms. A primal spark set the hairy mammal apart as man from the start. Hope centers on the present: now and here, the poem urges.
49695-motor-matt-s-close-call-or-the-sna:
Motor Matt's Close Call, or The Snare of Don Carlos is number seventeen of the Motor Stories, a weekly dime magazine of motor fiction from Street and Smith of New York. The number is dated June 19, 1909 and sold for five cents. The cover shows Motor Matt shouting for the colors to be raised, to see if the enemy dares fire on the flag.

Matt was a young hero of the new motor age, and his adventures ran on speed, nerve, and machinery. In this number a man named Don Carlos lays a snare for him, and treachery shadows the plot from the third chapter on. A serenade by his friend Carl opens the tale. It is fast, cheap, and thrilling, exactly what its readers paid a nickel for.
49991-the-first-book-of-eskimos:
Young readers meet the Eskimo peoples of the far north in a picture book from 1952. The writer and artist, who are not named on the title page, built the book from the reports of men and women who had lived in the Arctic. Their thanks page names the experts whose work they drew on and who checked the facts.

Those sources include Franz Boas, Vilhjalmur Stefansson, and Knud Rasmussen, three of the best known students of northern life. Ruth Bunzel of Columbia University read the draft and advised on it. Federal offices and the National Geographic also supplied facts and pictures. The result is a first book that grounds its picture of Eskimo life in the work of people who saw that life at first hand.
5077-marmion-a-tale-of-flodden-field-in-:
Sir Walter Scott's verse romance follows Lord Marmion, a proud English knight sent north on a mission in the days before the Battle of Flodden in 1513. Each of its six cantos opens with a personal address to a friend. Marmion then returns to his journey across border country, his schemes, and the people caught up in them.

Scott mixes invented intrigue with real history, building toward the famous and bloody battle on Flodden Field. Readers meet lovers, soldiers, nuns, and plotters along the way, and the poem's brisk storytelling has made it one of Scott's most widely read works of historical verse.
50816-dick-kent-with-the-eskimos:
Dick Kent with the Eskimos is a boys' adventure novel by Milton Richards, published at Akron, Ohio, by the Saalfield Publishing Company. The copyright page dates it to nineteen twenty seven in Roman numerals. Richards lists four earlier Dick Kent tales of the mounted police and the far north. A contents page promises Arctic action from the first chapter.

Chapter heads name a whalebone spear, a face in an ice window, and travel by kayak at sea. The hero is lost in Arctic fog, crosses a glacier, and hears an Indian bedtime story. A young Indian friend is dragged free of lodged snow in the front picture. Snow, ice, and northern peoples carry the plot.
51992-poems-1918-21-including-three-port:
Ezra Pound's Poems 1918-21, Including Three Portraits and Four Cantos, was published by Boni and Liveright at New York in 1921. A front list sets out Pound's books to date, from Provenca to Instigations. Some poems here had appeared in The Dial, The New Age, and The Little Review. The three portraits come first. The Homage to Sextus Propertius stands in twelve parts, and Langue d'Oc in five.

Hugh Selwyn Mauberley follows, in two parts dated 1919 and 1920. Its sections hold Yeux Glauques, Brennbaum, and Mr Nixon, with an envoi. The four cantos close the book: the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh. The Homage opens among the shades of Callimachus, bringing the Grecian orgies into Italy. Pound's volume marks his turn from short lyrics to the long poem that would fill his life.
53500-the-romance-of-the-ranchos:
E Palmer Conner wrote The Romance of the Ranchos. The Los Angeles Times first ran the pieces. Conner searched titles for a Los Angeles trust firm. His office stood at 433 South Spring Street. A fifth edition shows the work's reach. An old Plaza Church fronts the book.

Picture California cut into ranchos like a crazy quilt, he opens. Twenty-one missions dot that map in his view. A white hacienda stands on each rancho, he says. All doors stood open in welcome, he recalls. Americans took that land and tides of newcomers came. Ranchos traded for wine, groceries, and hides, he notes. One went for a lawyer's fee in his telling. Don Abel Stearns lost a vast rancho on honor. Title tales from the Spanish land grants give Los Angeles a past of deals, debts, and grace.
54072-indian-biography-vol-2-of-2-or-an-:
Indian Biography, volume two, was printed at New York in 1832 by Thatcher, a lawyer and writer on early American themes. The full title promises the lives of North American Indians marked out as speakers, warriors, statesmen, and other notable figures. This second volume takes up the New England tribes first. It opens with Indians who had submitted to Massachusetts, among them the Squaw Sachem of Medford.

Long chapter heads tell the reader what each life holds: Sagamore John and Sagamore James, their dealings with the English, and their deaths. Chickatabot, sachem of Neponset, gets a full account, from his war with the Squaw Sachem to his court appearances at Boston. Thatcher also weighs how Massachusetts treated the tribes beside the harsher record of Plymouth. The book mixes record, anecdote, and judgement, in the manner of its time.
54898-indian-biography-vol-1-of-2-or-an-:
Thatcher wrote Indian Biography, or an historical account of those individuals who have been distinguished among the North American natives as orators, warriors, statesmen, and other remarkable characters. Harper published it at New York in two volumes, this first volume in the eighteen thirties. The catalog title is a line of stars.

Benjamin Bussey Thatcher gathered lives of native leaders from the first contacts onward. Sachems, war captains, and treaty speakers fill his pages, drawn from colonial records and early histories. White readers of 1836, in the decade of removal, bought the book as both history and elegy. Thatcher's method is compilation with admiration. Many of his sketches preserve speeches and deeds found nowhere else so handy. Volume one begins a work still used by students of the early republic's native world.
55149-michigan-s-copper-country-in-early:
Michigan's Copper Country in Early Photos, by Tyler, is a picture book of the copper district. The Black Letter Press reprinted it at Grand Rapids in 1977. Nelson made the art work, and Cebelak adds a note dated March of that year.

Tyler says the scenes are best left unmarred by wordy description, since the eye grasps what language cannot. The winning of copper is the district's dominant industry and takes first place. Views show the depths of the mines and the great surface machinery that drives drills and hoists. Mills and smelters refine the metal into bullion, and wharves load ships for lower lake ports. One picture shows the old Cliff Mining Camp, once populous and now near deserted. Its houses, nearly half a century old, stare through bleak windows.
57130-chats-on-violoncellos:
Olga Racster wrote Chats on Violoncellos, with eighteen illustrations, issued in London by T Werner Laurie. Racster had earlier written Chats on Violins in the same Music Lover Library. She gave the book with love to her friend Mrs Blackett of Arbigland, from London in nineteen oh seven. A plate after Van Dyck, The Artist Wife, faces the title page. Chats, not dry chapters, structure the book.

The first chat opens with fog, the South Kensington Museum, the ravanastron, and Arabia. Racster traces the cello kin from old bowed instruments of East and West. Makers, players, and fine old cellos fill later chats in warm, gossipy prose. Music lovers get lore on wood, varnish, and tone without hard theory. The book suits a player who wants history at the fireside, not a manual.
58498-the-copernicus-of-antiquity-arista:
The Copernicus of Antiquity, Aristarchus of Samos, is Sir Thomas Heath's short life of the Greek astronomer who first set the earth moving around the sun. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge published it in London in 1920, in the Pioneers of Progress series on men of science, with Macmillan in New York. A diagram of Copernicus's system, anticipated by Aristarchus, illustrates the claim.

Heath divides his book in two. The first part sketches Greek astronomy up to Aristarchus, from Thales and Pythagoras through Plato, Eudoxus, and Heraclides of Pontus. The second treats Aristarchus himself: the heliocentric hypothesis, the apparent diameter of the sun, and his measures of the sizes and distances of the sun and moon. A bibliography and chronology close the volume. Heath, the great historian of Greek mathematics, wrote it for general readers.
59680-venus-to-the-venus-of-melos:
Auguste Rodin, the great French sculptor, wrote this prose hymn to the Venus de Milo. Dorothy Dudley translated it from the French, and it was published at New York in 1912. Drawings by Gertrude Huebsch accompany the text. Rodin addresses the statue herself, as a living presence.

He calls her modelled by the sea, calm with the calm of strength. Crowds from two worlds come to gaze at her, he says, and her twenty-five centuries seem only to have confirmed her youth. Mutilated, she remains entire to the artist's eye. The piece shows how the most famed statue of the ancient world worked on a modern master.
60506-powhatan-a-metrical-romance-in-sev:
Powhatan is a verse romance in seven cantos by Seba Smith. Harper and Brothers of New York issued the poem in eighteen forty one. Smith gives the book to the young people of the United States. He hopes it adds to sound joy and to mental culture there.

The preface takes on claims that poetry is a drug and a bore. Smith answers with a tale of a doctor and a sore arm. He denies that verse cannot sell or cannot be understood by readers. The Sidney motto on the title page praises tales that hold old and young. Readers get an early American long poem on a famed native chief.
60797-the-sheriff-of-pecos:
Bedford-Jones wrote The Sheriff of Pecos, a western tale printed at Garden City in 1923 after a run in the Street and Smith magazines. The tale opens in Mike's saloon in Pahrump County, where only three men stand besides Galway Mike behind his bar. One of them is Jack Robinson, and the talk soon turns to young Shumway's mortgage.

Buck lays plans, proofs are found, and masks come off in quick chapters. A mortgage held by a bank in Laredo County gives the villains their lever. Bedford-Jones wrote at tremendous speed for the pulps, and this short novel has his clean lines and sure pace. It ends, as the contents promise, with a trap sprung and a clean-up.
61217-1-492-633-marlon-brandos:
Vance Aandahl wrote a short science fiction tale whose title counts out more than a million Marlon Brandos. The tale ran in Worlds of If in September nineteen sixty-two. It opens at three in the morning in a neat suburban home.

Chester McRae, a mild man who works in accounts, wakes in a sweat and panic. He speaks and acts more and more like a tough film star, to his wife's shock. The story then cuts to his friend Bartholomew Oliver, a keen duck hunter. Short, sharp scenes build the joke and the threat. What has changed these plain men is the core puzzle.
61577-the-tahquitch-maiden-a-tale-of-the:
The Tahquitch Maiden, a tale of the San Jacintos by Phebe Estelle Spalding, was published in San Francisco in 1911. The catalog title is clipped to a scrap of the maiden's speech, but the title page gives the book's full name.

The story grows out of a camp in the San Jacinto Mountains of California. The narrator, resting in a hammock under old pines in Strawberry Valley, gazes up at Tahquitch Rock. The rock bears the name of a spirit of Native legend, who boasts in the motto that his people have died and been forgotten while he lives on in lasting youth. From that high camp and its looming peak, Spalding weaves the maiden's tale, mixing mountain scenery with the lore of the place.
61863-4-1-2b-eros:
Malcolm Jameson spins a space-trade tale in Planet Stories, Spring 1941. Captain Hank Karns, the Lone Trader, rides a sedan chair through rain in Venusberg. Two coolies splash through the muck roads at a lazy run.

Karns has just berthed his old trading tub, the Swapper. The port register shows trouble for an old friend. The Wanderer, Captain Wilkerson, lies detained by order of the Collector of the Port. Wilkerson himself sits in custody. Karns strokes his long white beard and thinks. Wilkerson is careful and upright, a lifelong friend. The headnote calls the tale's code, 4-1/2B, Eros, the key that broke the Mercury-Venus jinx. Jameson salts pulp adventure with port graft and cumshaw.
62139-captain-chaos:
Captain Chaos is a science fiction story by Nelson Bond, printed in Planet Stories in the summer of 1942. The Callisto-bound patrol ship Leo needs a cook. Its own cook falls ill on Phobos, the inner moon of Mars, after tasting his own cooking. Under sealed orders, the ship cannot turn back to Sand City spaceport.

The narrator, Dugan, is sent to hire a cook on the tiny settlement. But settlers hold good jobs, and war with the Outer Planets makes men shun a one-way trip on a rickety ship. The piping-voiced Jonah they finally ship jinxes the Leo straight into chaos, as the opening blurb promises.
62246-colossus-of-chaos:
Nelson Bond wrote a space tale that ran in Planet Stories in the winter of 1942. It was the evil spawn of lifeless space, drifting aimlessly until its sinister birthing place should come, the blurb warns. Finding that abode for life, it grew, sucking energy from Terra itself. Out of the darkness it came, out of the grim, bleak, frore depths of outer space into the empire of light and warmth and life.

It was like nothing known to man: round but not quite round, hard but not altogether hard, cold but not with the utter iciness of things from beyond. It did not move of its own will, for it was senseless, trusting chance to find it a resting place. It dropped to Earth unwatched and rolled a brief, sluggish way into a deep sandy pit. A thing from space wakes hungry here.
62498-castaways-of-eros:
Nelson Bond wrote "Castaways of Eros," a story printed in Planet Stories in the winter of 1943. Two families fight for the title to the asteroid Eros, and only one can win. One must outsmart the other, and both must beat the unscrupulous United Ores Corporation. The problem, says the blurb, is worthy of a Solomon.

Bobby stands at Long Island Spaceport wishing his father would stand a little straighter. The Patrolman beside Pop is broad and firm in his space blues, while Pop's chest caves in from studying things through a microscope. Mom calls Bobby to stop fidgeting. Bond, a prolific pulp writer, builds the claim dispute as family comedy, with an ending the embittered rivals could not foresee.
63054-hypatia-or-the-history-of-a-most-b:
Hypatia is an account of the learned woman of Alexandria, torn to pieces by a mob in the old tale. It was printed at London in 1753, at the price of sixpence. Three booksellers in Paternoster Row, Fleet Street, and Chancery Lane sold it. A plate shows Hypatia as an accomplished lady of parts.

The title page lays the murder on the clergy of Alexandria. Their archbishop Cyril is blamed for pride, emulation, and cruelty. The first chapter gives a general character of the lady herself. It names the contrivers and executioners of the barbarities she suffered. The authorities from which the story is drawn are listed there. This pamphlet is a famed attack on priestcraft in its age.
63649-the-temptress-la-tierra-de-todos:
Vicente Blasco Ibanez tells a tale of debts and beauty in The Temptress, in Spanish La Tierra de Todos, from E P Dutton of New York in 1923. Leo Ongley made the authorized translation. A publisher's list ranks it with The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse, Mare Nostrum, and Blood and Sand, and the printings ran to sixteen in July 1923 alone.

The tale opens with the Marquis de Torre Bianca rising late and facing his mail with dread. Paris letters mean creditors, reproaches, and threats. His wife, called The Fair Elena, takes such letters with perfect calm. Pride and debt collide.
63668-steel-giants-of-chaos:
Steel Giants of Chaos is a science fiction story by James R Adams. It appeared in Planet Stories in the winter of 1945. The blurb sets the stakes in five lines. Earth owed the Wronged Ones a world. Gene Drummond alone could repay that debt. Payment would save two races from extinction. Yet Drummond is a helpless prisoner of the very ones he wants to aid.

The story opens at New York Spaceport. Gene Drummond steps from his small scout ship onto Earth's soil. Fourteen gruelling months of biological research on Venus lie behind him. Venus's fatally poisoned air forced brief sallies from the ship. The noise and clamour of mechanics and stevedores feel like heaven. Fatboy the mechanic envies the trip to a restricted planet. Venus, Drummond says, is no paradise. A long vacation from strange worlds awaits, or so he plans.
63919-captain-chaos:
Captain Chaos, a science fiction story by Allen Morrissey, was printed in Planet Stories in November 1952. Science equipped David Corbin with borrowed time, its headnote says. It sent him winging out in suspension to future centuries. There a dark blue world's only defence was to seal tight the minds of foolish interlopers against prying.

Corbin wakes lying down in a small grey room, not knowing where he is. A voice from a speaker asks if he understands that his name is David Corbin. The name means nothing to him, and his thoughts come in a jumble. He finds himself naked save for heavy shorts, with no clue in any pocket. Morrissey builds the tale on lost memory and a stranger's borrowed life. Corbin must learn who he is, and why the future wants his mind shut, before he can act.
64214-princess-of-chaos:
Bryce Walton wrote this science fiction tale for Planet Stories in the spring of 1947. Moljar, a half-breed champion of Terran and Martian stock, stands in a blood-spattered arena. The howling mob hates him and prays for his death, but he looks coldly up at the Princess above.

He stands seven feet tall beside a dying saurian after three hours of the Red Moon Games. Blood and sweat run into his eyes under the blazing arc lights of the Colosseum. The dense Venusian air fills his lungs as he waits for the next thing sent against him, resolved not to die while she lives.
64549-my-arctic-journal-a-year-among-ice:
Josephine Diebitsch-Peary wrote My Arctic Journal, A Year Among Ice Fields and Eskimos, issued at London in 1894 by Longmans, Green. Robert E Peary, her husband, adds an account of the Great White Journey across Greenland. A front note tells of the steam whaler Kite. She sailed from New York on June 6, 1891, for Whale Sound in Greenland.

The Philadelphia Academy of Natural Sciences sent the party to winter there. Five members besides Peary and his wife made the smallest band ever sent for long Arctic work, the note says. Doctor F A Cook, Langdon Gibson, Eivind Astrup, and John T Verhoeff are named. Matthew Henson, Peary's attendant from Nicaragua work, went too. A relief party under Angelo Heilprin brought them home a year and a quarter later, lacking Verhoeff. Peary had crossed northern Greenland from coast to coast.
64992-narrative-of-henry-box-brown-who-e:
The Narrative of Henry Box Brown tells how Brown escaped from slavery enclosed in a box three feet long and two feet wide. The book was written from a statement of facts made by Brown himself, with remarks upon the remedy for slavery by Charles Stearns. It came out at Boston from Brown and Stearns, sold by Bela Marsh on Cornhill.

The preface swears the tale is not told to feed a prurient desire for some new thing. Brown, a Virginia slave, had himself crated and shipped by express to Philadelphia and freedom, at the risk of his life. Abolitionists printed his story as proof against slavery. Readers get one of the most famed escape narratives in full.
65417-cry-chaos:
Cry Chaos, a science fiction tale by Dwight Swain, ran in Imagination in September 1951. A blurb sets the stakes: the dark star held a dread secret that Gar Shane had to discover before our solar system was destroyed. But to go there meant certain death. The tale opens after the flight, with the hero dragged from his ship.

Men pry open the great silver ship's hatches at last and haul Shane out by his heels. They dump him face down in the gravel of the ramp. He is not a big man, but a spare, hard quality marks his close-knit body. Old scars tell of battles to the death with no quarter asked or given. Strange suns have burnt him dark; bluish pockmarks on his cheek speak of Pluto. His captors hang back in awe of the fallen great one.
68502-a-note-on-the-position-and-extent-:
Alfred Maudslay, a scholar of old Mexico, wrote this note on the great temple enclosure of Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital under Mexico City. It was printed in London in nineteen twelve. His subject is the walled sacred ground of the city and the teocalli, the temple pyramid of the war god Huitzilopochtli.

Maudslay weighs where the enclosure stood, how far it ran, and how the temple sat within it. He tests the earliest witnesses one by one. The anonymous conqueror who marched with Cortés gets a hearing, and so do the friars Motolinia and Sahagun, who lived among the Indians. Extracts from those old works are printed at the end. The note is dry, careful work: fixing a lost city's heart from words alone.
68671-sir-copp-a-poem-for-the-times-in-s:
Sir Copp is a satirical poem in six cantos by Thomas Clarke, issued at Chicago in 1867 in its sixth thousand. The book was entered for copyright in 1865. Clarke was the author of A Day in May and Life in the West. His motto calls truth the highest poetry and the bitterest satire.

The preface states a two fold object for the poem. It aims to photograph a phase of human depravity that beggars belief. It also aims to hand its subjects down to lasting infamy. A line quoted from the sixth canto mocks those who masked hypocrisy as young democracy. The poem belongs to the heated verse of the Civil War era. Clarke writes as a partisan with a whip in his hand, in rhymed cantos for the times.
69433-smugglers-island-and-the-devil-fir:
Smugglers' Island and the Devil Fires of San Moros is a children's adventure novel by Clarissa Kneeland, printed in Boston in 1915 with pictures by Wallace Goldsmith. The story is set in a small seaport town in Mexico, where Marian Hadley lives with her young brother Delbert. A school holiday gives the children their chance.

The children beg for a launch and sail to Smugglers' Island for a picnic that turns into a long stay. Storms, food troubles, a jaguar's track, and the building of a wickiup fill the chapters. One boy hunts for treasure-like finds while another goes after big game. The book is a hearty outdoor tale of pluck and teamwork for young readers of its day.
70489-a-true-exact-history-of-the-island:
A True and Exact History of the Island of Barbados was first published in 1657, one of the earliest English accounts of the island. The modern text replaces the long s of the original printing with the modern letter, and keeps the old spellings otherwise. The author describes the island's land, weather, plants, and the sugar works that were then making Barbados rich.

Early chapters of such histories list the fruits, trees, and beasts of the place and the diseases of new arrivals. The book is famous for its picture of planter life, hurricanes, and the making of sugar in the first age of the English Caribbean. Historians still mine it.
70850-ptolemy-s-tetrabiblos:
Ashmand translated Ptolemy's Tetrabiblos, the four books on the influence of the stars, from the Greek paraphrase of Proclus. Foulsham issued this new edition at London, with a preface, notes, and an appendix. The appendix adds extracts from the Almagest and the whole of Ptolemy's Centiloquy. The translation is dedicated, with profound admiration, to the author of Waverley. Byron's lines on the stars stand as its motto.

The advertisement defends the venture frankly. Astrology had been used in the poetical machinery of popular works, and readers wanted to know the system behind it. The first book lays the foundations: that knowledge may be had by astronomy to a certain extent, that prescience is useful, and how the planetary orbs act. Benefics and malefics, masculine and feminine, houses and triplicities follow. For a thousand years this was astrology's textbook, and Ashmand prints it whole.
73575-the-hounds-of-tindalos:
Frank Belknap Long wrote The Hounds of Tindalos for Weird Tales, where it ran in March nineteen twenty-nine. The tale is told by a friend who visits a man named Chalmers. Chalmers is pale, drawn, and deep in strange study. His desk holds the math of a noted physicist and sheets of odd geometric designs.

The narrator jokes that Einstein and John Dee make strange bedfellows in one room. That mix of new science and old magic sets the tone of the tale. Chalmers has pushed past safe bounds in his search through time and space. What comes for him gives the story its name. It is a short, tense work of weird horror.
73848-the-hero-of-the-filipinos:
Charles Edward Russell and Rodriguez wrote this life of José Rizal, the hero of the Filipino people. The book came out in New York and London in 1923, with photographs. They give it to the memory of Apolinario Mabini, a leader of the Philippine revolution.

Rizal was a poet, a doctor, and a novelist whose books woke his country under Spanish rule. Spain shot him in 1896, and he became a martyr to the cause of freedom. The authors note that the best lives of Rizal were shut away in Spanish or in rare Manila prints. Readers get a full English account of a man who fought an empire with a pen.
74152-life-and-religion-of-the-hindoos:
Joguth Chunder Gangooly, baptized Philip, wrote Life and Religion of the Hindoos, With a Sketch of My Life and Experience, issued at Boston in 1860. A front print, drawn by Mr Gangooly, shows ornaments worn by Hindu females. Necklaces, ear pieces, wrist bands, and arm bands are named and numbered. An editor's preface tells how the book was made.

The editor proposed the book and took on revision of the manuscript. He left it as Gangooly wrote it, with no betterments and no injuries, he pledges. Part of its interest lies in its style and peculiar modes of expression, he notes. He seldom ventured to correct even slips of grammar, he owns. Gangooly writes as a convert to Christianity who knew Hindu life from within. Faith, custom, and personal experience fill the volume for American church readers.
75026-the-wounded-eros:
The Wounded Eros is a book of sonnets issued in a limited edition of five hundred numbered copies. It was printed at the Riverside Press, Cambridge, uniform with The Spirit of Love and Other Poems. The author's other books include Two Gentlemen in Touraine, written as Richard Sudbury, and Among French Inns. Those works made his name as a lover of France.

In these sonnets, the author has set down the record of a passion. It makes one more of those stories of the heart written by the poets who joined the company of Sir Philip Sidney and his kind. The wounded god of the title is Love himself, and the sequence turns on his wound and the poet's. The fine limited dress, gilt top and numbered copies, marks the book as a collector's piece of the American fine-press age, as much keepsake as poem.
75438-corsairs-of-the-cosmos:
Edmond Hamilton wrote Corsairs of the Cosmos, a tale printed in Weird Tales in April nineteen thirty-four. The tale is told by Dur Nal, a captain in the Interstellar Patrol. A head note calls it a story of invasion from outside the universe.

Dur Nal and his two officers argue over their wildest adventure. One picks a fight with serpent-people, one a dark nebula, one a ride inside a comet. Their chief, Lacq Larus, settles it: the fight with the cosmic corsairs was the maddest of all. The tale starts as the cruiser returns to base at Canopus. It had patrolled a lonely stretch of the galaxy beyond Mira for long weeks.
77473-the-land-of-the-pueblos:
The Land of the Pueblos is a travel book on New Mexico by Susan Wallace, printed in New York in 1888 with illustrations. Wallace was the wife of Lew Wallace, governor of New Mexico and author of Ben-Hur. A front picture, from a sketch by the general, shows a Pueblo girl selling clay images.

Chapters take readers into Santa Fe, Pueblo towns, Mexican cottages, and old Spanish archives. Wallace rides to turquoise mines, tells tales of miners honest and otherwise, and visits the ruins of Montezuma's palace. Apache country and the dread Jornada del Muerto also appear. Her eye is sharp and her tone lively. The book is a rich early portrait of New Mexico's layered peoples and past.
77788-the-eyes-of-max-carrados:
Eyes of Max Carrados is a set of detective tales by Ernest Bramah. George Doran published it in New York with rights held in 1924. Bramah also wrote The Wallet of Kai Lung and Kai Lung's Golden Hours. Nine cases fill the contents after a long introduction to the hero. The Virginiola Fraud opens the case list at page thirty three.

Later cases treat a vanished Marie Severe and the secret of Dunstan's Tower. A poisoned dish of mushrooms and a ghost at Massingham Mansions follow. A missing actress, an ingenious Mister Spinola, and a spy case raise the pace. An Eastern mystery closes the set of Carrados puzzles and deductions. Carrados solves by mind what his blind eyes cannot see at all.
78024-the-woman-of-andros:
The Woman of Andros, by Thornton Wilder, was published in New York in 1930. A note at the front gives its roots. The first part rests on the Andria, a comedy by Terence. Terence in turn used two lost Greek plays by Menander. The tale opens as night creeps along the Mediterranean Sea. Gibraltar holds a last gleam of red and orange. Storm plays about Sicily while the Nile mouth lies still as wet pavement.

The island of Brynos, happy and little famed, takes the evening breeze. Women chatter, boys shout, and lambs cry in the harbour town. Simo and Chremes, the chief fathers, linger at a wineshop game. Wilder gives an old plot a still, bright prose of his own.
8257-the-world-english-bible-web-amos:
Amos was a shepherd and fig farmer from the southern village of Tekoa who traveled north to preach in Israel during a time of wealth and ease. He had no training as a prophet, and he said so plainly. His message was blunt: the rich crushed the poor, courts took bribes, and fine religious festivals meant nothing while justice was trampled in the streets.

The book opens with judgments on Israel's neighbors, then turns the same fire on Israel itself, and closes with visions of a plumb line, a basket of ripe fruit, and ruin. A final promise of restoration softens the end. Amos remains the Bible's plainest voice for social justice, quoted whenever worship and fairness are set against each other.
britannica-1911-algae-benthos:
Benthos, a section of the Algae article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, treats the algae that live attached to a surface. Most algae grow in that fixed way, like land plants rooted to a substratum. The comparison then turns careful. A land plant's root both anchors the plant and draws up water, but an alga, bathed in water holding dissolved food, absorbs through its whole surface.

Attachment alone is what the alga needs, so its gripping organ is better called a holdfast than a root. Holdfasts vary widely in structure, often forming a single flattened disc, as in the Fucaceae. Rocks and boulders are the favourite ground for marine algae. The section notes how fast harbour walls, piles, and pontoons of stone, wood, and iron become covered with growth. Shipowners would welcome any cure for the fouling of hulls by algae.
britannica-1911-andros:
Andros is a Greek island at the north end of the Cyclades. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its form and ancient ties. It lies southeast of Euboea and north of Tenos. The island runs nearly twenty-five miles long.

Hills cover most of its face, cut by rich watered valleys. About eighteen thousand people lived there at the time. The chief town on the east coast held some two thousand. Ruins of the old capital stand on the west coast. Its famed temple there honored the wine god Bacchus. Ionian settlers with Thracian blood filled the island early. It grew rich enough to plant towns across the sea. Athens, Macedon, and Egypt fought over it in turn. Venice shielded it for centuries before Turkish rule.
britannica-1911-apollos:
Apollos, a figure of the early church, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was a Jew of Alexandria, his name being a short form of Apollonius. After Paul's first visit to Corinth, Apollos worked there in a like way. Later he was with Paul at Ephesus, the entry notes from Paul's letters.

Those letters tell of four parties in the Corinth church, two of which took the names of Paul and Apollos. The split can hardly have come from clashing doctrines, the article says. The book of Acts shows Apollos speaking and teaching with power and success. He may have won hearers by a teaching of wisdom in an allegorical style. The entry also weighs a seeming clash in the Acts account of his knowledge of the faith.
britannica-1911-arany-janos:
János Arany (1817–1882) was Hungary's greatest poet after Petöfi. He was born at Nagy-Szalontá in March 1817. His parents were small Calvinist yeomen. Their property was a thatched cottage and plot. He was an only, late-born son. Chapel hymns and prayers filled his childhood. His precocity was remarkable from the start. At six he entered school at Szalontá.

He read everything within reach there. Hungarian and Latin both fed him. Preceptor posts followed at Kis-Ujszállás and Debreczen. He taught himself French and German meanwhile. Scholastic monotony eventually drove him away. He joined a troupe of travelling actors. Conscience pangs plagued him on the road. His father had meant him for the pastorate. The entry follows his return and poetic rise. Translations of Toldi and Buda's Death are listed.
britannica-1911-asbestos:
Asbestos, a fire proof thread stone, is set out in a long earth entry in the 1911 Britannica. Its name comes from a Greek word for that which cannot be quenched. Old Greeks used that word for quicklime, but Pliny used it in our sense. In old days it was at times woven into cloth goods. Shrouds of it kept corpse ash apart from wood ash at a burn rite.

Threads of the stone shift much in kind from bed to bed. Soft silk like threads bear the name mountain flax in trade talk. Felted beds of it bear names such as mountain leather and cork. Most trade stock now comes from a snake stone kind with short strong threads. Canada leads the trade, with beds in Quebec worked since eighteen seventy seven.
britannica-1911-athos:
Athos is a place article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Mount Athos is the easternmost of three long points of land reaching south from Macedonia. They run into the Aegean Sea like the prongs of a trident. The peak rises like a pyramid, capped with white marble.

The summit stands 6350 feet high and can be seen from far away. At sunset it shows from the plain of Troy and from the slopes of Olympus. On the isthmus lie traces of the canal Xerxes cut before invading Greece. The entry praises the beauty of the peninsula's scenery. Its special interest lies in its monks: a unique group of communities with medieval customs. Their treasures of Byzantine art and stores of old documents are also named. Readers get both a mountain's shape and the strange holy world upon it.
britannica-1911-bacsanyi-janos:
Bacsanyi, Janos (1763-1845), was a Hungarian poet born at Tapolcza who published his first work, a patriotic poem on the valour of the Magyars, in 1785. That year brought him a treasury clerk's post at Kaschau, where with two fellow patriots he edited the Magyar Museum until the government suppressed it in 1792.

The clerkship went next, and in 1794 his part in Bishop Martinovich's conspiracy put him in the Spielberg state prison for two years. Vienna, a bank post, and marriage followed; then, in 1809, translating Napoleon's proclamation to the Magyars drove him to refuge in Paris. After Napoleon's fall Austria let him live at Linz on condition he never leave it. His collected poems appeared at Pest in 1827, and he died at Linz in 1845.
britannica-1911-barbados:
Barbados is an island article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an island in the British West Indies. It lies seventy-eight miles east of Saint Vincent and is twenty-one miles long. At its broadest it spans about fourteen miles, and it covers 166 square miles. Coral reefs ring its coasts, in places reaching three miles out to sea.

The island is raised but not mountainous. Near its centre stands Mount Hillaby, at eleven hundred feet, its highest point. From there the land falls on all sides in a series of terraces to the sea. The slopes are so gentle that a drive over its good roads shows hardly any climb. Its one natural harbour is Carlisle Bay, on the south-west coast. That bay is little more than a shallow roadstead, open only to light vessels.
britannica-1911-bathos:
Bathos is a Greek word meaning depth, the bottom or lowest part of anything, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains. In plain first use, then, it named a physical depth, the floor of a thing rather than its top. Nothing in that first sense pointed to writing or speech at all, and the word could be used of any fall from a high place to a low one.

Writing gave bathos its sharp modern sense. It now names an anticlimax, a drop in literature or speech from the sublime to the ridiculous, from high matter to flat, common stuff. That use, the entry says, comes from Pope's satire on Bathos in the Miscellanies of 1727–1728, which he called “the art of sinking in poetry.” Pope's title mocked Longinus's famed essay On the Sublime, turning praise of height in writing into a joke about sinking.
britannica-1911-campos:
Campos, an inland city in the state of Rio de Janeiro in Brazil, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It stands on the Parahyba River, thirty miles from the sea. Its count in 1890 was 22,518 in the city and far more in the wider town lands. Small steamers can sail the river above and below the town.

Sand bars at the river mouth bar coast ships, so a port sixty miles off serves Campos by rail. The city sits just sixty nine feet above the sea. It lies at the west edge of a rich plain given to sugar cane. The air is hot and damp, and fruit of the tropics grows in plenty there. Rail lines link it to the capital.
britannica-1911-chios:
Chios is an island off the west coast of Asia Minor. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica praises its wine, figs, and gum. Turks called it Saki Adasi, and Italians knew it as Scio. About sixty-four thousand people lived there at the time.

The island runs about thirty miles long and up to fifteen wide. Oranges, olives, and even palms grow in its mild air. Its northwest wine won fame in the ancient world. A Chian smith of the seventh century before Christ found how to weld iron. Chian sculptors in marble also held a high name. Epic singers called Homeridae kept Homer text on the island. That link gave Chios a claim as the poet birthplace.
britannica-1911-cienfuegos:
Cienfuegos, originally Fernandina de Jagua, is one of the principal cities of Cuba, in Santa Clara province on the south coast, 195 miles east-south-east of Havana. Its people numbered 30,100 in 1907, and steamers link it with Santiago, Batabanó, Trinidad and the Isle of Pines. It lies six miles from the sea on a peninsula in the landlocked bay of Jagua. Vessels drawing 16 feet reach its wharves directly.

Broad regular streets, a handsome cathedral and the Tomas Terry theatre mark the city, which has gas and electric light and a full water supply. Rich sugar estates, among the largest in the world, surround it, and sugar and tobacco lead its trade. General Luis de Clouet founded the city in 1819, and a hurricane forced rebuilding in 1825. Columbus had visited the bay long before.
britannica-1911-coptos:
Coptos, in Egyptian Keft or Kebto, is the modern Kuft, a village with a rail station near the west bank of the Nile. It stands about 25 miles north-east of Thebes. In old times it was an ancient city and capital of the fifth nome of Upper Egypt. Roads to the Red Sea set out from its gates. One road ran due east to Kosseir past the old quarries of Hammamat.

Trade with Arabia and India raised the city to great wealth in time. Berenice, founded by Ptolemy Philadelphus, drew some traffic south in its day. In the year 292 Coptos joined a revolt against Diocletian. Near total ruin fell on it for that act. It rose again as a place of note and a seat of Christians. Traffic in time shifted to nearby Kus. For part of the 600s it bore the name Justinianopolis. Its local god was Min.
britannica-1911-coraes-adamantios:
Adamantios Coraës, a Greek scholar and patriot who lived from 1748 to 1833, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Smyrna, a merchant's son, he shone as a boy in ancient Greek. From 1772 to 1779 he ran his father's business at Amsterdam. When that business failed he went to Montpellier and studied medicine for six years, living by translation work.

He then settled in Paris till his death in 1833. Fired by the French Revolution, he worked for Greek freedom from Turkish rule. His great aim was to teach the Greeks to see the works of old Greece as their own birthright. He sought to clean the written tongue and enrich it with classic words, and under his lead the language of books drew close to pure Attic. His chief works are his editions of Greek authors.
britannica-1911-cos:
Cos is an island near the south west corner of Asia Minor. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its other names as Stanko and, in Turkish, Istan keui. It runs about twenty five miles long at the Budrum bay mouth. Nearly all of its ten thousand people were Greeks at that time.

A limestone ridge chain lines its south coast with little break. Dry heights contrast with rich lowland soil in its fields of grain. Sultana raisins from its vines win the island its chief fame abroad. Grapes sail to Egypt in local boats as a top export in trade. Its one town holds a knights fortress and a famed plane tree.
britannica-1911-delos:
Delos is an island article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a small island in the Aegean Sea. It is the smallest but most famed of the Cyclades, the ring of islands said in old belief to stand in a near circle round it. The island is a rough mass of granite, about three miles long. Near its centre it rises to Mount Cynthus, some 350 feet high.

The article notes that Delos now has no trees, only brush and a few patches of corn land farmed by men from Myconus. It then turns to the digs run by the French School at Athens since 1877, led chiefly by Homolle. For a reader, the entry joins hard facts about a bare rock to rich finds that made it a key site for Greek studies.
britannica-1911-enos:
Enos, in old form Aenos, is described in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica as a town of Turkey in Europe. It lay in the district of Adrianople. The town stood on the south shore of the river Maritza, where the stream spreads out to meet the Aegean Sea in the Gulf of Enos. Its count in nineteen hundred and five was about eight thousand.

Enos holds a ridge of rock ringed by broad marsh land. It is the seat of a Greek bishop, and most of its folk are Greek. Trade was once strong here, thanks to the river mouth post on the great water road from Adrianople to the sea. That trade has since fallen off. Sick air, sand banks that now bar all but small craft, and a rival port with a rail link all hurt it. The note is a crisp case of a port in decline.
britannica-1911-erdelyi-janos:
János Erdélyi, who lived from 1814 to 1868, was a Hungarian poet and author born at Kapos. The 1911 Britannica article says he was schooled at the Protestant college of Sárospatak. In 1833 he moved to Pest. Six years later the Hungarian Academy of Sciences elected him a member. His fame rests on his great store of Hungarian folk poems and tales. That work came out in 1846 and 1847, put forth by the Kisfaludy Society.

Erdélyi also made a vast book of Hungarian proverbs for the same society, printed in 1851. For a time he ran a review of fine letters. In 1848 he was named head of the national theatre at Pest. After 1849 he lived in his home town, where he died in January 1868. A last folk store came out the year after his death. It holds three hundred songs, nineteen tales, and 7,362 proverbs.
britannica-1911-garay-janos:
János Garay (1812–1853) was a Hungarian poet and author, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lists his early works. He was born on the tenth of October 1812 at Szegszárd, in the county of Tolna. He studied at Fünfkirchen from 1823 to 1828, then at the university of Pest. In 1834 he brought out a heroic poem in hexameters, titled Csatár.

Plays on themes from Hungarian history followed in quick order. Among the most successful were Arbócz, Országh Ilona, and Báthori Erzsébet. The first two were printed at Pest in 1837, and the last in 1840. Garay was also a busy journalist. In 1838 he moved to Pressburg to edit the political journal Hirnök, the Herald. He came back to Pest in 1839 and was elected a corresponding member of the Hungarian Academy.
britannica-1911-jerez-de-los-caballeros:
Jeréz de los Caballeros, a town of south-western Spain, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in the province of Badajoz, on two heights above the river Ardila. The Portuguese frontier lies twelve miles west of it. The census of 1900 counted 10,271 people there.

A Moorish wall with six gates rings the old town. The newer part is regularly built, planted with orange trees. No railway reaches Jeréz, and its commerce stays small. Its staple trade is in farm produce from the country round. Ham and bacon lead, from swine herds reared in the oak forests. The town is said to have been founded in 1229 by a king of Leon. His son gave it to the Knights Templar a few years later. From those knights it takes its proud surname, Jeréz of the Knights.
britannica-1911-koumoundouros-alexandros:
Alexandros Koumoundouros (1814–1883) was a Greek statesman, born in 1814. His studies at the university of Athens were broken again and again by lack of money, and he began work as a clerk. He took part in the Cretan rising of 1841 and in the move of 1843 that won a constitution from King Otto. He then practised law at Kalamata. Elected to the chamber in 1851, he rose fast, held the president's chair by 1855, and served as minister of finance in 1856, 1857 and 1859.

Koumoundouros became prime minister in March 1865 and formed several later governments as power swung between him and Tricoupi. During the Cretan rising of 1866–68 he made active warlike plans against Turkey, but King George dismissed him, judging that Greece could not act alone. In power again in 1880, he had to cut back his demands and accept the limited gains in Thessaly and Epirus made in July 1881. His ministry fell in 1882.
britannica-1911-martos:
Martos is a town of southern Spain, in the province of Jaen, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies sixteen miles west of Jaen on a rail line, and its people numbered 17,078 in 1900. The town stands on a west peak of the Jabalcuz hills. A ruined castle crowns the peak, and the plain of Andalusia spreads below.

Two sulphur springs near the town have bathing houses. Trade is near all in farm goods. Martos may stand on or near the site of the Tucci of Ptolemy, which Rome made strong and named anew. Ferdinand the Third took it from the Moors in 1225 and gave it to the knights of Calatrava. In 1312 two brothers of that order were put to death there by the king's command.
britannica-1911-melissus-of-samos:
Melissus of Samos is the subject of a thinker article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Melissus was a Greek thinker of the Eleatic school. He was born probably not later than 470 years before Christ. One old source calls him a political leader in his home town. The same source says he led the fleet that beat Athens in 442.

The article turns to his writings, kept in parts by later authors. They defend the teaching of Parmenides in long chains of argument. Being, he says, is without end or start. It cannot come from nothing, and it cannot pass into nothing. What has no end must be one and without change. It can have no split inside, for a split would need empty space, and empty space is nothing. The text notes the clash this logic makes with what the senses report.
britannica-1911-melos:
Melos, now called Milo, is an isle of the Aegean Sea in this 1911 Britannica place entry. It sits at the south west edge of the Cyclades group. Fire rock forms the isle, with ash, hard lava, and glass stone in its beds. A deep port cuts in from the north west and near splits it in two. That port is the bowl of its old fire mouth.

Hot sour springs steam on the east shore of the port. Sulphur, alum, mill stones, and salt rank as its old wealth. Farms grow vines, cotton, and barley on its dry soil. Old town ruins hold a Roman stage house and fine carved finds. The famed Aphrodite of Melos came from this soil. Its glass stone made it a hub of early sea trade.
britannica-1911-morelos:
Morelos, an inland state of Mexico, is laid out in a place entry in the 1911 Britannica. It lies south of the Federal District, on the south slope of the high plain. Puebla, Guerrero, and Mexico ring it on three sides. Its folk count for nineteen hundred was one hundred sixty one thousand six hundred ninety seven. Ranges from the Sierra de Ajusco break its land into vales that open south.

Weather shifts fast with height, from cold damp tops to hot low vales. Light rain means most farms must water their fields by hand work. Yet the state ranks high for crops such as sugar, rice, corn, and beans grown as coffee. Mines for gold and silver sit idle and left, the text says. Two rail lines cross the state from the capital.
britannica-1911-moriscos:
Moriscos, meaning little Moors, was the name given to the Spanish Muslims who accepted baptism, and to their children, as this 1911 Britannica article explains. Many were in fact of the same stock as the Christians, sprung from converts to Islam. Muslims who kept their faith under Christian rulers were called Mudéjars, and for long they worshipped freely under treaties.

That freedom shrank after the fall of Granada in 1492, though its terms had secured free worship. The Catholic kings sought one faith among their subjects, and the Church pressed the same aim. A first archbishop made some gains by gentle means, but harsh steps at the end of 1499 sparked revolt. By 1525 open Islam was stamped out across Spain, and the Moriscos' hard work in the fields drew envy from their Christian neighbours.
britannica-1911-moxos: Moxos, also written Mojos or Mohos, is the name of a tribe of South American Indians, and this very short 1911 Britannica entry gives their place and story in brief. They live around the headwaters of the Madeira river in northern Bolivia, on both sides of the Mamoré. They once submitted to Inca rule, yet in 1564 they boldly drove back the Spaniards. A century later they welcomed the Jesuits and became devout Catholics. Their number is given as some thirty thousand.
britannica-1911-nicephorus-callistus-xan:
Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a Greek church historian. He was of Constantinople and was the last of his line of historians. He flourished from about 1320 to 1330. His Ecclesiastical History fills eighteen books in all. It brings the narrative down to the year 610. For the first four centuries he depends largely on predecessors. Eusebius, Socrates, Sozomen, Theodoret, and Evagrius are named.

His additions for that early period show little critical faculty. For the later period his labours are much more valuable. They rest on documents now no longer extant. He had free access to those documents in his time. A table of contents for five more books exists. Those books would continue the history to 911. Whether they were ever actually written is doubtful. Some scholars hold he passed off another man's work as his own.
britannica-1911-pherecydes-of-leros:
Pherecydes of Leros, a Greek writer of myths who flourished at about 454 before Christ, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He is most likely the same man as Pherecydes of Athens. The two are split apart by some old lists, yet the entry treats them as one. He was born on the island of Leros, it seems.

He was called an Athenian since he spent most of his life in Athens and wrote his great work there. Three treatises of his, on Leros, on Iphigeneia, and on the festivals of Dionysus, are lost in full. Many fragments of his family trees of gods and heroes do survive in later books. That work ran to ten books in the Ionic tongue. He reshaped legends to fit common belief, not to strip them down to reason.
britannica-1911-pherecydes-of-syros:
Pherecydes of Syros is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a Greek thinker. He worked in the sixth century before Christ. Some lists count him among the Seven Wise Men. He is said to have taught Pythagoras. With one possible bar, he was the first Greek prose writer. He moved in the circle of Peisistratus at Athens. He also founded a group linked to Orphic belief.

Later writers credit him with two large claims. One is the doctrine that souls pass to new bodies. The other is that the soul does not die at all. Cicero and Augustine call him the first to teach that. His study of the sun left a cave on Syros. That cave, the heliotropion, marked the sun's yearly turning point. It became one of the sights of the island.
britannica-1911-romanos:
Romanos was a Greek hymn writer called the Pindar of rhythmic poetry. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places his birth at Emesa in Syria. He served as deacon at Berytus, then moved to Constantinople in time. Church posts at Blachernae and Cyrus held his later service there.

Legend tells that the Virgin gave him a scroll to eat in sleep. Waking on Christmas Day, he sang his famed Nativity hymn at once. He is said to have written more than one thousand hymns in all. Themes range from church feasts to saints lives and last judgment. An editor quoted calls him the greatest poet of the Byzantine age.
britannica-1911-ros:
Ros, or De Ros, names a noble English family traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Robert de Ros, who died in 1227, opens the line in the account. He was a son of Everard de Ros of Helmsley in Yorkshire. Lands in Yorkshire and in Normandy both lay in his hands.

He served King John in several ways at home and abroad. Northumberland lands came to him, and there he built a castle at Wark. At about 1215 he broke with the king and joined the barons in revolt. He stood among the twenty five men set to uphold Magna Carta. He fought John when the king cast that charter aside in bad faith. In time he made his peace with Henry the Third and became a monk before his death. His wife was a daughter of William the Lion, king of Scotland.
britannica-1911-sahos:
The Sahos, also called Shonos, are the subject of a brief peoples entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. They are Africans of Hamitic stock living west of Massawa. Some authorities regard them as true Abyssinians. More probably, the entry says, they are akin to the Gallas and Afars.

Most Sahos are Muslims, while a few are Christians. That is nearly the whole of the hosted text, which runs to only a few lines. It records the two views of their kinship without settling the question. Readers who need more are left to the linked entries on the neighbouring peoples named in the text.
britannica-1911-samos:
Samos is an island in the Aegean Sea described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is one of the chief and richest isles that lie close to the mainland of Asia Minor. A strait of about a mile parts it from that shore. The isle runs about twenty-seven miles long and fourteen miles at its widest.

A range of hills fills most of its length, and its highest peak, Mount Kerkis, rises more than four thousand seven hundred feet. The isle paid a small yearly sum to Turkey but was in practice a free principality. A prince of Greek birth, named by the Porte, ruled with a senate and a chamber of deputies. The seat of rule was Vathy. The soil is rich, and much of it is set with vines. The wine of Vathy grapes had a high name. The isle held about fifty-five thousand folk in 1900.
britannica-1911-simonides-of-amorgos:
Simonides of Amorgos was a Greek poet of sharp verse who wrote in the mid part of the seventh age before Christ. He was born on Samos and took his name from a town he helped found on a near isle. He left two books of such verse and some songs of grief. About thirty bits of his sharp verse still live.

His verse is clear and strong, and its sting is aimed at faults in all, not at one man. One famed piece sorts kinds of wives by beast type. The neat wife is drawn from the bee, while the worst is drawn from the ape. Praise for the good wife ends that piece.
britannica-1911-tharros:
Tharros, an old town of Sardinia on the west coast, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stood on a narrow sandy neck at the north end of the Gulf of Oristano. The tower of San Giovanni di Sinis now marks the spot. It lay twelve miles west of Othoca by the coast road.

The town began as a Phoenician place and lived on into Roman times. The Saracens destroyed it in the eleventh century. Scant Roman ruins and a road of large stone blocks can still be seen. Part of the site now lies under the sea. Its large burial ground shows how much the town once mattered. Digging there began in earnest in 1838, and Phoenician tombs came to light in 1850.
britannica-1911-thasos:
Thasos is an island in the north of the Aegean Sea, and its early settlers open a history in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica.
